documents.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in entrepreneurship, research on its impact remains fragmented. To address this limitation, we provide an integrative, entrepreneur‐centered review of how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: (1) opportunity recognition and ideation, (2) opportunity evaluation and commitment, (3) resource assembly and mobilization, and (4) venture launch and growth. Based on our review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework, which not only catalogs GenAI's benefits and costs throughout the entrepreneurial process but also identifies potential trade‐offs underlying GenAI's double‐edged role. For example, GenAI may improve venture idea quality yet produce hallucinations and biases; boost entrepreneurial self‐efficacy yet heighten overconfidence; increase functional breadth and self‐sufficiency yet reduce prosociality; and enhance productivity yet diminish cognitive engagement, learning, and memory. We also identify features of GenAI that underlie these empowering and entrapping effects. Moreover, we explore boundary conditions that moderate GenAI's effects, including entrepreneurs' expertise, approaches to GenAI use, and personal traits and values. Beyond these theoretical contributions, our review and framework offer practical guidance for entrepreneurs seeking to use GenAI strategically while managing its risks. Managerial Summary We review how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: opportunity recognition and ideation, opportunity evaluation and commitment, resource assembly and mobilization, and venture launch and growth. Based on this review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework to help entrepreneurs understand GenAI's trade‐offs at each stage. The future of entrepreneurship will depend less on whether entrepreneurs use GenAI than on how they use it. Used thoughtfully, GenAI may empower entrepreneurs by expanding their capabilities to engage in entrepreneurial activities. Used uncritically, GenAI may entrap entrepreneurs by restricting or eroding those capabilities. Entrepreneurs should therefore verify what GenAI produces, calibrate GenAI use to their expertise and task demands, and decide which tasks to delegate to GenAI while retaining human judgment for consequential decisions.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and $τ$-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.

Large language model (LLM) serving systems dynamically batch user requests for GPU execution, so the same request may be processed alongside different requests across runs. If the GPU kernels lack batch invariance (BI), this changing batch context can alter the numerical output for an unchanged input, undermining reproducibility. Existing kernel generation agents focus on correctness and efficiency but \emph{overlook BI}. We find 19 confirmed BI violations among 83 batch-applicable released artifacts. To address this limitation, we propose \tool, which combines contract-guided static dependency analysis with dynamic validation of bitwise consistency across batch contexts. \tool is designed as a plug-in component for general kernel agents, allowing their original optimization capabilities to be reused while adding BI enforcement. We integrate it as successive acceptance gates in the optimization loop, rejecting structurally risky or dynamically non-invariant candidates before performance benchmarking and returning feedback to the agent. Experiments across three agent frameworks under baseline and BI-aware generation on real world LLM serving tasks show that \tool improves the BI pass rate from 67.6\% to 91.9\% while retaining 91.8\% of the baseline geometric mean speedup. These results demonstrate that \tool can be incorporated into kernel optimization by agents as an additional reliability objective alongside correctness and speed.

Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.

GraphRAG systems often use knowledge graphs to retrieve relevant context for an LLM that produces the final answer. That makes answers more inscrutable and therefore less appealing for domains where transparency is paramount. We present GraphRAGProv, an architecture that executes SPARQL queries over source-grounded RDF graphs to compute answers and their how-provenance polynomials. These polynomials record which statement occurrences were used and how they were combined. Because each occurrence is linked to its source text, users can follow these links to check whether the extracted statements reflect the text and whether the query combines them to answer the question. Querying thereby becomes a way to inspect and evaluate the text-to-graph transformation. Our interactive demo examines 400 cases from two multi-hop QA benchmarks, revealing extraction and query errors even when the final answer is correct.

This evidence-based practice project explored structured group activities to support cognitive engagement, social interaction, and well-being among assisted living and memory care residents with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias. Drawing on cognitive stimulation, reminiscence, and Montessori-based care, recommendations included music, memory games, creative activities, and meaningful daily tasks adapted to residents’ interests and abilities. Staff education emphasized supportive prompts, resident choice, and assistance to encourage participation, independence, dignity, and person-centered care.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has shown strong empirical gains in improving the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) on tasks such as mathematics and programming. However, recent studies have shown that RLVR rollouts often collapse onto a narrow set of reasoning trajectories, limiting the explored reasoning space. Motivated by findings that thinking tokens at critical steps serve as critical structural elements in LLM reasoning pathways, we propose Guided-RLVR, a novel approach that augments RLVR with a lightweight controller. The controller strategically injects semantically meaningful steering tokens into the sampling distribution, encouraging the model to approach problems from multiple reasoning perspectives and thereby expanding the exploration space. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Guided-RLVR consistently outperforms existing RLVR methods while producing more diverse reasoning trajectories.

Despite advancements in cryptographic techniques such as homomorphic encryption, blockchain, attribute-based encryption and quantum-resistant algorithms that aim to enhance privacy and trust in healthcare, significant ethical and technical issues remain. This chapter fills that gap by systematically examining vulnerabilities related to algorithmic logic, mathematical fragility, randomness generation and human misimplementation. Using case studies from real and simulated healthcare environments, it explores how encryption mistakes, biased artificial intelligence (AI) generated keys or restricted data access can threaten both patients and healthcare providers. The findings align with existing security standards, indicating that cryptographic failures are often sociotechnical rather than purely technical problems. The chapter emphasises that protecting patient data effectively requires not only technical solutions but also ethical governance frameworks that promote transparency, continuous auditing and human oversight in the design of cryptography. Looking ahead, the chapter underscores the importance of incorporating ethics-by-design principles and fostering collaboration among engineers, ethicists and policymakers to ensure future healthcare cryptography safeguards both digital security and human dignity.

Purpose This study examines how control allocation between users and artificial intelligence (AI) systems shapes reuse intention in AI-enabled travel planning and whether this effect operates through user experience (UX), cognitive reappraisal, expressive suppression, psychological empowerment and satisfaction. Design/methodology/approach Two scenario-based studies were conducted. A laboratory pilot (n = 92) validated system-dominant, shared-control and user-dominant planning conditions. A main online study (n = 463) tested the proposed serial process using confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling and 5,000-resample bootstrapping. Findings Control allocation significantly affected UX. More favorable UX increased cognitive reappraisal and reduced expressive suppression, and these two regulatory routes had opposite effects on psychological empowerment. Empowerment enhanced satisfaction, which subsequently predicted reuse intention. A supplementary analysis further indicated that AI usage experience conditioned the relationships between UX and emotion regulation. Practical implications AI travel planners should treat control allocation as an interaction-design decision. Modular editing, progressive explanations, reversible changes and adaptive control can preserve user agency while retaining the efficiency benefits of AI assistance. Originality/value This study extends continuance research by identifying the upstream psychological process through which satisfaction is formed under different control-allocation structures. It further distinguishes UX as an evaluative appraisal from emotion regulation as a subsequent coping process in AI-enabled travel planning.

An on-road experiment with 27 drivers across 50 horizontal curves examined the association between radius and visual psychophysiological workload on a mountainous two-lane highway. Pupil-area change rate, fixation intensity, heart-rate change rate, and heart-rate variability (SDNN) were combined using factor analysis and entropy weighting. Crossed linear mixed-effects models used driver and curve section as random intercepts and radius as a continuous predictor. Smaller radii were generally associated with higher pupil, fixation, and heart-rate responses and lower SDNN. Among linear, quadratic, cubic, and logarithmic forms, the logarithmic comprehensive-load model fit best (AIC = −2511.47; BIC = −2485.43), with a significant radius effect (β = −0.2968, 95% CI: −0.3283 to −0.2653, p < 0.001). Successive-curve inconsistency was not independently significant (p = 0.976). Within 45.83–900.83 m, exploratory workload boundaries were approximately 75, 150, 270, and 500 m. These are preliminary human-factors screening values, not design standards or validated comfort thresholds.

Whilst technology has the potential to deliver significant benefits to older and disabled people, enabling greater mobility and independence, it may also leave them unable or unwilling to engage with it, or lacking in trust. Understanding how people engage with technology in relation to their mobility is the core aim of this chapter. To understand how people engage with technology, we need to know who they are and enough about them to understand how and why they do or do not engage, and we also need to know about the features of the technology that encourage or discourage engagement. Thus, part 1 addresses older people and how they think and behave in relation to technology; this includes their motivation, attitudes and beliefs and how their cognitive abilities interact with possible uses of technology and whether there is a digital divide. Part 2 addresses the issues associated with the technology that make it easier or harder to use, and more or less likely for people to engage with; this includes what we know about how people actually engage in terms of ergonomics, which includes the perceptual and cognitive elements of the technology.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: This study aimed to examine how EFL learners' trust in AI feedback, AI-related anxiety, and AI literacy relate to their engagement with, and uptake of, AI-mediated written corrective feedback. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design combined survey data from 300 university EFL learners, analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), with follow-up semi-structured interviews (n = 16); the structural model explained 48% of the variance in feedback uptake. AI literacy positively predicted trust (β = .46) and negatively predicted anxiety (β = -.39); trust was the strongest positive predictor of both engagement (β = .41) and uptake (β = .44), while anxiety exerted smaller negative effects. A cluster analysis identified three learner profiles - Confident Collaborators, Anxious Verifiers, and Detached Low-Literacy Users. Because anxiety was measured at three points across the period of AI-mediated collaboration, change over time was also examined: a repeated-measures ANOVA showed AI anxiety declining significantly across the three waves (partial η² = .18), and a latent growth curve model showed that higher AI literacy and higher trust each predicted a steeper decline. The qualitative findings showed that learners did not accept AI feedback uncritically but practised calibrated trust, verifying machine feedback against teachers and peers, and that AI literacy functioned as a regulating resource that tempered both over-reliance and anxiety. On this basis the study proposes a Calibrated Trust Framework for AI-mediated assessment, in which AI literacy supports calibrated trust, calibrated trust drives engagement, and engagement converts into uptake. The study advances a learner-centred account of human-AI collaboration in language assessment and argues that AI literacy, rather than tool sophistication alone, is central to responsible, pedagogically meaningful, AI-mediated assessment. Implications for assessment design, teacher education, and ethical practice are discussed.

Brain-to-AI Interfacing (B2AI) offers a novel human-centered neurotechnology framework for augmented cognition. In this proof-of-concept feasibility case study, we demonstrate a working non-invasive B2AI prototype supporting bidirectional communication between a user and a large language model (LLM) through EEG-based input and TMS-based feedback. In a virtual navigation task, we found that use of the B2AI system was associated with higher path efficiency in a single-user case study. Additionally, we found that the average time per step was higher when the system was active, likely reflecting the time required to initiate the EEG command, query the AI module, receive TMS feedback, and execute the instructed movement. Together, these findings suggest that the B2AI system was technically feasible and may support more efficient task performance under constrained experimental conditions. Future work and fully powered experiments will be needed to determine the generalizability, usability, safety, and application value of the system, but this case study suggests that current technology supports the use of B2AI as an experimental tool for augmented cognition research.

The original roots of the information society (jōhō shakai) are clearly Japanese and date back to the year 1963. The concept was developed in the context of a private study group circle spearheaded by the anthropologist Umesao Tadao, including members like the science fiction writer Komatsu Sakyō and the futurologist Hayashi Yūjirō. Drawing on the methodology of science and technology studies (STS), I will show how the ideological narrative underlying Umesao’s original theory on the information industries was condensed into a sociotechnical imaginary (STI) in the years from 1963 to the end of the 1970s. This article explains why the narrative was so successful and how the Expo 1970 in Osaka served as a showcase for the public performance and stabilization of the STI. The article argues that this contributed to its lasting impact on the way in which Japanese technofutures were imagined, based on the premise of a techno-centered society.

The modern Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) is undergoing a profound paradigm shift driven by the rapid maturation of generative artificial intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), and automated program synthesis engines. While historical transitions—from linear Waterfall models to Agile sprints and continuous DevOps pipelines—focused primarily on procedural orchestration and organizational agility, the integration of Artificial Intelligence introduces cognitive automation directly into the engineering fabric. This research paper presents an exhaustive empirical and methodological investigation into the impact of AI across the end-to-end SDLC, evaluating its tangible ramifications on developer productivity, cognitive workflow dynamics, code quality engineering, and enterprise security. Employing a rigorous triangulated mixed-methods research design, this study combines: (i) quantitative repository mining across 1,200,000 commits spanning 45 enterprise software projects; (ii) a controlled randomized quasi-experiment comprising N = 120 professional software engineers measuring task velocity and cognitive workload via the NASA-TLX inventory; and (iii) longitudinal static analysis tracking post-release defect density and Common Weakness Enumerations (CWE). Our findings demonstrate that AI assistance compresses coding lead times by 55.8% and accelerates developer flow states, yielding substantial improvements across DORA deployment frequency and change velocity metrics. However, ungoverned AI code generation introduces acute quality paradoxes, including a 19.4% surge in code churn, subtle logic regression risks, and elevated vulnerabilities in insecure deserialization and unverified package dependencies. To resolve this tension, we propose a multi-tier Enterprise AI-Augmented SDLC (A-SDLC) Framework coupling Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) policy guardrails, local context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), automated mutation test synthesis, and continuous AIOps observability. Finally, we analyze organizational governance imperatives, intellectual property licensing risks, and emerging horizons in autonomous multi-agent coding swarms, establishing an empirical blueprint for resilient, high-assurance software engineering.

Purpose – This paper examines the impact of virtual property tours and allied digital technologies — including 3D/360-degree walkthroughs, augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), artificial intelligence (AI)-based recommendation engines and digital mortgage integration — on home-buying decisions. It explores how these technologies are reshaping buyer search behaviour, trust formation, engagement and speed of decision-making, with specific reference to an internship undertaken at House of Real Estate. Design/methodology/approach – The study adopts an exploratory-descriptive design carried out in two phases, a structure informed by the bibliometric-cum-qualitative approach used in prior beauty-influencer marketing research (Shukla and Jha, 2026). Phase I consists of a secondary literature and industry-data review covering global and Indian PropTech adoption trends. Phase II proposes a primary, survey-based investigation to be administered among prospective home buyers and site-visit leads generated by House of Real Estate, structured around the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory and the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB). Findings – The secondary evidence indicates that virtual tours and immersive technologies increase listing engagement, shorten time-on-market, encourage remote and out-of-town buyers to shortlist properties faster, and support (but do not replace) the final in-person evaluation before purchase. Adoption is strongest among younger, digitally native buyers and in metro markets, while tier-II/III markets continue to show gaps in digital trust and literacy. Research limitations/implications – The paper is primarily literature- and internship-observation based; the proposed primary survey instrument (Appendix A) requires field administration to generate statistically validated, House of Real Estate-specific results. Findings should therefore be read as a conceptual and directional foundation rather than a conclusive empirical outcome. Originality/value – The paper extends the growing PropTech literature by explicitly linking virtual-tour adoption to the stages of the buyer decision journey, and by translating this into actionable recommendations for a real estate brand's marketing and sales strategy. Keywords – Virtual property tours, PropTech, home-buying decisions, virtual reality, augmented reality, technology adoption, real estate marketing, consumer behaviour.

RESUMOObjetivo: descrever o perfil e a concentração das coberturas extraordinárias da equipe de enfermagem hospitalar, comparar sua frequência entre grupos de motivos e analisar os fatores associados ao custo por evento. Métodos: estudo longitudinal retrospectivo baseado em registros administrativos individuais de janeiro de 2024 a maio de 2026, em hospital privado de alta complexidade da região Centro-Oeste do Brasil. Dos 2.416 registros identificados, 2.093 compuseram a coorte principal após exclusões sequenciais por categoria não elegível, motivo ou setor não informado, período indefinido e potenciais duplicidades. Os valores foram corrigidos pelo Índice Nacional de Preços ao Consumidor Amplo para reais de maio de 2026. O custo por evento foi analisado por modelo linear generalizado com distribuição Gamma e ligação log, e a frequência mensal por grupo gerencial foi comparada por regressão binomial negativa com erros-padrão agrupados por mês. Resultados: o custo real acumulado foi de R$ 468.056,88, com média de R$ 223,63 por evento. Vacâncias e afastamentos prolongados, ausências não programadas e ausências programadas concentraram 91,5% dos eventos e 92,9% dos custos. Vacâncias e afastamentos prolongados tiveram custo unitário ajustado 5,7% menor que as ausências programadas, porém frequência mensal 2,10 vezes maior; as ausências não programadas foram 1,88 vez mais frequentes que as programadas. As coberturas de enfermeiros tiveram custo ajustado 50,0% maior que as de técnicos de enfermagem. Conclusão: o impacto financeiro decorreu sobretudo da recorrência de déficits estruturais e de ausências não programadas, mais do que do custo unitário, que reflete principalmente a tabela de remuneração. A classificação sistemática das causas permite direcionar ações de recrutamento, planejamento de férias, saúde ocupacional e mecanismos internos de cobertura.Palavras-chave: Absenteísmo; Recursos Humanos de Enfermagem no Hospital; Custos Hospitalares; Administração Hospitalar; Admissão e Escalonamento de Pessoal. Financial impact and factors associated with the cost of extraordinary coverage in the hospital nursing workforce ABSTRACTObjective: to describe the profile and concentration of extraordinary coverage in the hospital nursing workforce, compare its frequency across groups of reasons, and analyze factors associated with cost per event. Methods: retrospective longitudinal study based on individual administrative records from January 2024 to May 2026 in a private high-complexity hospital in the Brazilian Midwest. Of 2,416 records identified, 2,093 composed the primary cohort after sequential exclusion of ineligible categories, missing reason or target unit, undefined coverage period and potential duplicates. Monetary values were adjusted by the Brazilian Extended National Consumer Price Index to May 2026 reais. Cost per event was assessed with a generalized linear model with Gamma distribution and log link, and monthly frequency by managerial group was compared with negative binomial regression with standard errors clustered by month. Results: the cumulative real cost was BRL 468,056.88, with a mean of BRL 223.63 per event. Vacancies and prolonged leaves, unplanned absences and planned absences accounted for 91.5% of events and 92.9% of costs. Vacancies and prolonged leaves had a 5.7% lower adjusted unit cost than planned absences, but a 2.10-fold higher monthly frequency; unplanned absences were 1.88 times more frequent than planned absences. Coverage by registered nurses had a 50.0% higher adjusted cost than coverage by nursing technicians. Conclusion: financial impact resulted mainly from the recurrence of structural staffing gaps and unplanned absences rather than from unit cost, which mainly reflects the payment table. Systematic classification of causes can guide recruitment, vacation planning, occupational health and internal coverage mechanisms.Keywords: Absenteeism; Nursing Staff, Hospital; Hospital Costs; Hospital Administration; Personnel Staffing and Scheduling.

Based on the urgent need to cultivate occupational health action ability in recent years, this study adopted the key Objectives and Key Results (OKR) to explore the practical effect of its application in the comprehensive experimental teaching of“Occupational health and occupational medicine (OHOM)”. We made full use of existing teaching resources, promoted the reform of experimental teaching, and improved the experimental teaching level and experimental ability of undergraduate students majoring in preventive medicine. We randomly selected 60 fourth‑year undergraduate students from two classes of the preventive medicine major to carry out the comprehensive experimental teaching of OHOM. The traditional teaching mode and OKR assessment method were used respectively to observe the teaching effect. There were 15 males (50.00%) and 15 females (50.00%) in the control group. There were 17 males (56.67%) and 13 females (43.33%) in the study group. We established an OKR teaching model for the comprehensive dust exposure experiment in the course of OHOM, including the design of teaching procedures, the arrangement of key steps, and specific evaluation methods. Through practical exploration, we found that in the OKR teaching experimental group, 26.67% and 23.33% of students respectively believed that this teaching mode could improve their learning efficiency and comprehensive learning ability. We obtained a certain understanding of students’ mastery of experimental knowledge and found that the experimental group had a significantly greater mastery of experimental knowledge than the control group did, and OKR had an obvious effect on students’ mastery of experimental knowledge. On the other hand, through the OKR teaching method, students’ learning satisfaction is significantly improved. Both traditional teaching mode and OKR evaluation method have good teaching effect, OKR teaching effect is better than traditional teaching method, comprehensive experiment score is significantly higher than traditional method ( P < 0.05). The practical teaching of the OHOM comprehensive experimental course highlights, to a certain extent, the advantages of its professional characteristics, strengthens the teaching of experimental skills, and integrates the OKR assessment method. It can serve as an important supplement to and resource expansion of traditional classroom learning, and holds considerable value for promotion in improving the quality of comprehensive experimental teaching.

Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used to monitor brain activity in both clinical and research settings. However, conventional scalp EEG systems require multiple electrodes, specialised equipment, and trained personnel, which limits their practicality for long-term monitoring in everyday environments. In-ear EEG has emerged as a promising wearable alternative that enables discreet and portable neural monitoring. This systematic review examines the current state of research on in-ear EEG technologies. Twenty-four studies met the inclusion criteria and were analysed thematically. The literature highlights rapid progress in device miniaturisation and wearable design, with reported applications including sleep monitoring, seizure detection, cognitive workload assessment, fatigue monitoring, and emotion recognition. Despite these advances, challenges remain related to signal quality, spatial coverage, and motion artefacts. Further research is required to validate in-ear EEG for broader clinical and real-world applications.

Research Aim: This study aims to analyze the role of Artificial Intelligence in shaping inclusive leadership and to formulate strategies for strengthening local wisdom as a foundation for sustainable leadership. Design/Methods/Approach: The study employs a Literature Review approach, synthesizing scholarly works from Scopus, Web of Science, and Sinta (2010–2026). Thematic analysis is used to identify patterns and relationships among inclusive leadership, AI, and local wisdom. Research Finding: The findings reveal that inclusive leadership plays a critical role in bridging technological advancement and human values. It enhances employee engagement, innovation, and decision-making quality while mitigating algorithmic bias. Additionally, integrating local wisdom strengthens ethical governance, social legitimacy, and organizational sustainability through value-based and culturally grounded practices. Theoretical Contribution/Originality: This research offers a novel integrative framework combining AI, inclusive leadership, and local wisdom, addressing the gap between technological and humanistic perspectives in leadership studies. Practitioner/Policy Implication: The study provides strategic guidance for leaders and policymakers to implement human-centered AI, promote inclusivity, and embed cultural values into digital transformation. Research Limitation: This study relies on secondary data; future research should incorporate empirical validation and sector-specific analysis.

The article analyzes the Russians’ assessments of information security issues related to neural networks amid a shift in the emphasis of their use from professional practices to personal ones, while parallel or hybrid use is possessed. Drawing on OLS regression, the relationship between the intensity of neural network usage and the Russians’ assessments of neural network security is identified. With large language models as a case study, the Kruskal–Wallis test has been chosen to appoint a significance of the differences in assessments of their information security across the groups distributed by gender, age, and education level. The obtained results testify to the uniformity of critical attitude towards the information security apart from gender or age and the presence of statistically significant differences by education level. A contradiction between the adoption of large language models as a tool and the perception of low user security is highlighted. The study notes the advisability of embedding user protection mechanisms directly into the neural network interfaces.

Background: Pediatric trauma and medical resuscitations require fast thinking, organized teamwork, and clear communication. Video review has long been used to improve performance, but it has traditionally been led by physicians. As nurses, we carry a detailed understanding of bedside workflow and the realities of resuscitation that often isn’t fully captured in these reviews. Bringing nurses directly into the video review process offers a chance to create more meaningful discussions, highlight important operational details, and build a stronger, shared understanding of what actually happens during high-stress events. Objectives: Through this presentation, participants will: • To introduce a video review model that intentionally and meaningfully includes emergency nurses in case analysis. • To show how nursing perspectives improve team communication, situational awareness, and understanding of trauma and resuscitation workflows. • To identify themes and insights that emerge when nurses participate fully in the review process. • To highlight how this collaborative approach supports ongoing improvement in emergency care and team performance. Methods: From the start of the video review program in our pediatric emergency department, nurses were included as equal partners. Nursing, physician, and quality improvement leaders worked together to build the structure, goals, and expectations for the program. We established shared learning principles, emphasized psychological safety, and encouraged open, honest communication. Nursing staff helped identify which workflow and communication elements should be prioritized during review. Sessions were co-facilitated by nursing and medical leadership to ensure balanced discussion and representation. Themes were collected through observation of group dialogue, recurring patterns across cases, and reflections shared by participants. Results: Including nurses significantly enriched the discussions. Nurses frequently pointed out workflow issues, equipment readiness concerns, and communication gaps that had not been consistently recognized in physician-driven reviews. Their input improved role clarity, supported more reliable communication practices, and highlighted the cognitive load and rapid task-switching required at the bedside during pediatric trauma and medical resuscitations. Participants reported better cross-disciplinary understanding, increased confidence in speaking up, and a renewed sense of teamwork. The collaborative model offered a more complete picture of resuscitation care and supported ongoing professional growth. Implications and lessons learned: Bringing nurses into video review creates a more inclusive and realistic way to learn from actual resuscitations. Key takeaways include the need to establish psychological safety, provide structure for guided discussion, and recognize the unique contributions of each team member. Integrating nursing perspectives strengthens communication, supports shared mental models, and reinforces the essential role of nurses in high-acuity care.

ABSTRACT A narrow view of fire safety often overlooks the complex web of factors that shape the real‐world risks for building occupants, community members, people in temporary shelter, and those without housing. Many studies examine individual components of fire safety, such as fire hazards, building performance, and human behavior. However, there has been limited interrogation of the complex interactions between the fire hazard, building (shelter), and human factors, with even less including the social and cultural components. Research that crosses these boundaries in a suitably joined‐up way is scarce. Ignoring these intersections often leads to siloed fire safety interventions that fail to capture the dynamic and systemic nature of fire risk, perpetuating the lack of interdisciplinarity and representation in the fire safety field. Traditional multi‐ or interdisciplinary approaches often struggle to overcome disciplinary boundaries or institutional constraints, resulting in continued siloed understanding of the fire problem. This paper argues that a convergence approach, one that fosters collaboration across technical, social, and human‐centered domains, is essential for understanding and addressing fire risk holistically. We take the first steps towards outlining such a framework by drawing on a case study of fire risk in buildings and shelters. Through this example we show how different perspectives can be brought together to capture the complexity of fire safety challenges, proposing a clear direction for developing integrated, equitable, and more effective approaches to fire risk reduction.

documents.abstract: The importance of cloud computing lies in its provision as a critical infrastructure for large-scale applications and emerging technologies. Modern cloud computing infrastructures demand efficient resource orchestration for dynamic workloads and service-level agreement requirements. In this regard, traditional scheduling techniques are not efficient. This study proposes a novel intelligent resource orchestration framework based on hybrid artificial intelligence techniques that combine deep learning, reinforcement learning, and optimization algorithms for efficient resource management. The proposed architecture has different layers for analytics, decision engines, and orchestration functions that enable efficient resource management. Experimental results confirm that the proposed framework improves resource usage efficiency, task completion time, and operational cost efficiency for large-scale cloud computing infrastructures. The hybrid AI-based orchestration technique is efficient for scalability and adaptability for future cloud computing.

Beyond AI Sandboxes and Permission Checks: A Technical Specification for Cross-Platform AI Execution Finality, Hardware Security, and Interoperability New here? Download the presentation first for a quick visual overview, then the full specification. The problem AI agents no longer just generate text. They run code, call APIs, operate browsers, move money, and control devices across iOS, Android, desktop, cloud, and hardware. An agent can be sandboxed, logged in, and approved by a permission check, and still lack the authority to cause the specific effect it is about to cause, at the moment that effect occurs. Sandboxes limit where an agent runs. Permission checks approve categories of action. Neither binds authority to the actual operation presented at the point where it takes effect. The core idea Computation is not authority to act. The specification treats computing an action and making it effective as separate, independently verified steps: Candidate Act → Non-Effective State → Protected Validation → Scoped Finality Authority → Finality Sink Verification → Controlled Effectuation A proposed operation stays non-effective until an independent Finality Sink reconstructs the actual operation and verifies protected evidence and scoped, non-bearer, single-use authority. If any check fails, the effect does not happen. What the specification covers AI-agent security: tool execution, prompt-injection containment, external-action authorization iOS, Android, and cross-platform interoperability for third-party AI tools Agent gateways, sandbox egress, credential release, and non-bypassable enforcement Trusted execution environments, kernel mediation, virtualization, and hardware command boundaries Multi-agent delegation, causal dependencies, conflicting operations, and revocation Cloud, enterprise, financial, robotics, and safety-relevant systems The full document contains the detailed embodiments, definitions, workflows, and algorithms. Run it yourself: reference implementation with 400 automated tests https://github.com/sangmdas/ios-android-ai-execution-finality A vendor-neutral Python and SQLite reference model of the core workflow. All 400 tests pass. It demonstrates: the exact SHA-256 commitment of a Candidate Act and its Non-Effective State; operation-bound authority checks: principal, tenant, route, resource, quota, expiry, and generation; independent Finality Sink verification of the actual operation; single-use scoped authority and replay prevention; revocation and ownership epochs; atomic consumption, plus crash and lost-acknowledgement recovery; causal receipts between dependent operations. bash git clone https://github.com/sangmdas/ios-android-ai-execution-finality cd ios-android-ai-execution-finality python -m pip install -e . python -m pytest -q # 400 passed The model is platform-neutral. It does not include privileged iOS or Android system hooks, TEE or hardware enforcement, or cross-system atomic transactions. Those mechanisms are described in the specification. See docs/LIMITATIONS.md in the repository. Independent review is welcome through GitHub Issues and Discussions. Relay and reseller APIs have become a common way to access large language models (LLMs), yet users cannot directly verify whether they receive the models they request and pay for. This opacity motivates LLM relay auditing, but existing methods struggle to combine low cost, robustness to benign deployment changes, and statistically interpretable decisions under black-box access. To address these limitations, we propose distributional fingerprint auditing (DFA), a statistical method that requires only textual responses from suspect and trusted reference endpoints. DFA repeatedly queries semantically simple finite-choice probes and uses the resulting categorical response distributions to construct endpoint fingerprints. It compares the suspect and reference fingerprints probe by probe and aggregates the resulting evidence using the Cauchy combination test, yielding an approximate endpoint-level $p$-value for audit decisions at a prespecified nominal significance level. Using registered fingerprints of candidate models, a likelihood-based formulation further supports model attribution under full substitution and joint estimation of substitute identity and substitution ratio under constant-ratio mixed routing. Our benchmark includes 16 proprietary and open-weight LLMs from 10 model families. Across 240 ordered full-substitution pairs, DFA achieves high detection rates at a nominal significance level of $α=0.05$, using five probes and 250 relay requests per audit with stored reference fingerprints. Configuration overrides can lead to rejection even when the served model remains unchanged, with effects varying across models and configurations. Simulations based on stored empirical fingerprints demonstrate accurate model attribution and estimate substitution ratios, with estimation error decreasing as the audit budget increases.

documents.abstract: Discourse parsing based on Segmented Discourse Representation Theory (SDRT) is crucial for capturing the structural dynamics of dialogues. However, most prior research focuses on English, and its effectiveness for Japanese remains unclear owing to the lack of Japanese SDRT corpora. To address this issue, we construct Japanese SDRT corpora by translating existing English SDRT corpora using an LLM. Through a comparative evaluation of prompt-based and fine-tuned LLMs, we show that the models achieve comparable performance between English and Japanese, suggesting the cross-lingual applicability of SDRT-based discourse parsing. In order to investigate why the English and Japanese parsers achieve similar performance, we conduct ablation analyses on discourse markers and contextual inputs. Our results reveal that most of the Japanese discourse markers we examined have little impact, and the models' predictions depend heavily on contextual discourse relations rather than on the content of the context clauses. This structural reliance might explain the comparable performance despite the substantial typological differences between English and Japanese.

A small number of GPU kernels often determines the efficiency of large language model training and inference. High-performance kernel development typically relies on expert knowledge through manual implementation, collaboration with general-purpose models, or specialized agents equipped with domain knowledge, evaluation methods, and search workflows. We investigate how much value this knowledge provides as foundation models become stronger. We introduce JustGoal, a goal-only baseline in which a general-purpose agent receives only the optimization objective and constraints, without kernel-specific infrastructure, knowledge bases, or predefined workflows, and builds its own evaluation loop. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, JustGoal outperforms open-source libraries on 8 of 10 operators, achieving per-operator geometric mean speedups of 1.14x to 2.34x. It also surpasses the fastest publicly released specialized-agent kernel on 5 of 9 operators with available comparisons. In a controlled same-model comparison using Fable 5.1 on single shapes, the KDA-0.5 harness reaches 0.95x of JustGoal's performance, while single-mechanism ablations show no consistent benefit from domain knowledge or predefined workflows. These results indicate that specialized machinery should be justified by clear gains over a same-model, same-scope goal-only baseline and reevaluated whenever the foundation model changes.

The adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies presents significant opportunities to enhance occupational safety and health (OSH) management within modern methods of construction (MMC). However, organisations often lack clarity on which factors are crucial for the adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies for OSH improvement in MMC. Existing studies have mainly investigated individual technologies, adoption barriers, or organisational capability factors, without systematically identifying and prioritising the comprehensive set of people, organisational, technological, and infrastructure attributes that enable effective Industry 4.0-enabled OSH management in MMC. This study addresses this gap by identifying, validating, and prioritising the key attributes for effective Industry 4.0-enabled OSH management in MMC using a four-stage methodological approach comprising SLR, expert verification, Delphi method, and voting analytic hierarchy process (VAHP). Through a combination of systematic literature review (SLR) and expert verification, 21 attributes were identified and grouped into four clusters: people, organisation, technology, and infrastructure. The 21 identified and validated attributes were then ranked by a group of experts through a two-round Delphi survey. Following this, the weights and importance of attributes were determined using the voting analytical hierarchy process (VAHP). The results indicate that organisation and people clusters achieved the highest relative priorities; Management support, workforce competence, and technology acceptance were identified as the highest-priority attributes. These findings reveal a sociotechnical hierarchy in which organisational and human capabilities are prioritised above technological and infrastructural capabilities, suggesting successful Industry 4.0-enabled transformation for OSH improvement depends more on social-subsystem capability than on technology deployment alone.

documents.abstract: Coordinating multiple recommendation objectives (e.g., click and conversion) is critical for real-world generative recommendation (GR). However, since a positive item in GR can be retrieved only when its tokens are successively selected at every decoding step, traditional item-wise methods lack fine-grained token-wise supervision to guide intermediate steps. Motivated by its success in foundation models, we consider introducing multi-objective on-policy distillation (MOPD) into GR to distill two single-objective teachers into a student at each token. Yet, we find that in vanilla MOPD, (i) teachers exhibit unequal distillation difficulty at each token (i.e., token-level imbalance), and (ii) the harder-to-distill teacher varies across tokens (i.e., cross-token inconsistency), leaving each objective poorly learned at certain steps and hindering positive item retrieval for both objectives, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this challenge, we propose KL-MOPD (KL-Weighted Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation), a simple yet effective distillation method that allocates token-wise teacher weights proportional to the initial student-teacher token-wise KL divergences, thereby strengthening supervision for the harder-to-distill teacher at every decoding step. Despite its simplicity, we theoretically prove that KL-MOPD strictly outperforms vanilla MOPD in the additive joint recommendation objective under mild conditions. Moreover, KL-MOPD is plug-and-play and computationally efficient, requiring only a one-time pre-training weight calibration with negligible training overhead. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks, a billion-scale industrial dataset, and online A/B tests on our e-commerce advertising platform demonstrate that KL-MOPD significantly improves both individual and joint recommendation performance. The anonymous code is provided for peer review.

BACKGROUND: Shared decision-making (SDM) is a core competency in patient-centered care, yet it is challenging for physicians. Simulation-based education with standardized patients (SPs) offers valuable practice opportunities for undergraduate medical education (UME), but is limited by cost, scalability, and variable feedback quality. Advances in large language model (LLM) technology and virtual patient (VP) design present a promising pathway toward accessible, realistic, and high-quality SDM skill training. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to develop LLM-powered, real-time interactive 3D avatars for SDM training in UME and to evaluate their acceptance among undergraduate medical students. METHODS: We conducted a descriptive, cross-sectional mixed methods study at KU Leuven, Belgium (November-December 2025). The avatar system was developed through an iterative, interdisciplinary collaboration between medical educators, SDM experts, software developers, user experience designers, and AI engineers, grounded in prior work on physicians' educational needs and SDM learning mechanisms. Development comprised prototype case authoring, usability testing with medical students, and iterative refinement. The final system is a web-based platform featuring real-time, LLM-powered spoken dialogue with diverse, photorealistic 3D patient avatars; layered prompts configuring avatar personality, clinical scenario, and difficulty; an educator panel for case authoring; and automated AI-generated formative feedback structured around 6 phases of SDM. After using the system for 1 month, a convenience sample of UME students completed a 9-item, 5-point Likert scale questionnaire grounded in the technology acceptance model (TAM), assessing perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and intention to use. Optional open-text responses were narratively analyzed to triangulate these findings. RESULTS: Of 25 recruited participants, 24 were included in the analysis. Internal consistency was acceptable for perceived usefulness (α=0.76) and intention to use (α=0.78), but not for perceived ease of use (α=0.69). All construct means exceeded the scale midpoint of 3, suggesting high overall acceptance. Students rated perceived usefulness highest (mean 4.43, SD 0.50), followed by intention to use (mean 4.42, SD 0.59), and perceived ease of use was the lowest (mean 3.81, SD 0.68). Fourteen participants provided open-text responses. These highlighted the value of a safe, low-pressure environment for practicing communication without patients or peers present; reported mixed experiences with avatar realism, with reservations directed at behavioral rather than physical realism; and identified technical difficulties (microphone issues, freezing, and crashes) as the most frequent area for improvement. CONCLUSIONS: LLM-powered, real-time interactive 3D avatars are feasible and well-accepted tools for SDM training in UME. Students found the system educationally valuable and intended to use it again. Technical reliability and behavioral realism should be prioritized in future development. The modular architecture and automated feedback pipeline support scalable deployment across disciplines, institutions, and languages. Larger, multi-institutional studies with objective learning outcome measures are needed to establish efficacy.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) models for ranking typically adopt a fast-thinking direct prediction paradigm with strong practical efficiency. However, ranking requires fine-grained scoring across multiple candidate items, while existing GR models still mainly rely on one-shot prediction. This raises the question whether additional inference-time computation can further improve ranking quality. Recently, inspired by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models (LLMs), some work has begun to introduce reasoning into recommendation systems. Some of these methods rely on LLM reasoning frameworks to perform explicit reasoning in textual space, but such designs are not suitable for more widely deployed non-textual recommendation models. A more relevant direction is to introduce latent reasoning into ID-based recommendation models. Although recent work has extended latent reasoning to industrial ranking, how successive reasoning steps should improve fine-grained candidate scores remains less explored. To address this problem, we propose Refiner, a latent residual reasoning framework with parameter-efficient fine-tuning for generative ranking. Our approach introduces three key components: (1) a residual reasoning mechanism that progressively refines ranking scores through cumulative additive corrections, (2) history queries that provide condensed user behavior representations to enhance candidate-specific reasoning, and (3) a parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy that leverages LoRA modules to adapt pre-trained models for latent reasoning. Extensive experiments on two public benchmarks, an offline industrial dataset, and an online A/B test demonstrate that Refiner consistently improves over direct prediction, validating its effectiveness and practical utility.

Haptic cues intended to support development of a manual skill may hold advantages over verbal cues in that they are delivered directly to the learner’s hands and can shape the movement directly, whereas a verbal cue must first be decoded and translated into a motor command. Haptic guidance has improved learning of steering and timing tasks, with the largest gains among learners of lower initial skill or facing greater difficulty. To test our hypothesis that haptic cueing will improve performance in a manual learning task better than verbal cueing, we compared the performance of three participant groups at backing a hitched trailer. The first group received Haptic, the second Verbal cues, and the third group received No Assistance. Preliminary results show the benefits of assistance, but so far without significant differences between the Haptic and Verbal groups.

Decision models offer fast choices over sup- plied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models interpret open-ended tasks through flexible generation and reasoning at the cost of sequential decoding. Many work- loads expect a generative backend to determine what can be done and therefore provide no well-defined candidate list. We bridge this in- terface gap with a small candidate formalizer trained on offline teacher-generated lists. The formalizer constructs explicit, validated alter- natives from task context, and a frozen deci- sion model selects an entry. A motivating com- parison with official TypeSafe Jev-1.13.0 on 200 CALVIN-D test episodes reports 11% suc- cess with generic motions versus 46.5% with DeepSeek V4 Flash pose candidates. Sepa- rately, a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 CALVIN-D validation annotations finds that a locally deployed decision model can achieve at most 52.6% task success rate with the fine-tuned formalizer, compared with 11.8% without it, and the end-to-end latency is kept to 2.09 s, whereas Qwen3.5-27B is 3.67 s with the exact experiment setting.

Large language models have recently shown strong potential for automatically optimizing GPU kernels, yet their effectiveness depends critically on the hardware information available to the kernel optimization model. Existing systems typically rely on predefined profiling strategies, leaving what to profile largely outside the optimization process. We show that effective profiling is not simply about collecting more information: increasing the number of profiling metrics does not monotonically improve kernel optimization, while the most useful profiling information varies across kernels. Our theoretical analysis further shows that, under such heterogeneous profiling utility, kernel-conditioned selection can outperform any single fixed profiling configuration. Motivated by this observation, we propose AutoProfiler, a feedback-driven framework for learning a deterministic profiling tree from optimization feedback. The tree is iteratively refined through REWRITE and SPLIT operations, with an LLM generating candidate modifications and empirical evaluation determining their acceptance. Once constructed, the tree quickly gathers the required profiling information for any kernel, allowing the LLM rewriter to be invoked only once. Experiments on KernelBench show that our approach improves kernel optimization over fixed profiling configurations under constrained profiling budgets. These results suggest that hardware profiling should evolve from static metric collection toward profiling reasoning, making profiling itself a new dimension for improving kernel optimization. The codes are available at https://github.com/Satissss/AutoProfiler.

Health system innovations aimed at improving healthcare access are complex with potential for unintended consequences. There is a need for real-time evaluation which captures evolving contexts and impacts. This study presents experiences—both successes and failures—at extending the sensemaking methodology from our previous work into a large scale health ecosystem for monitoring, evaluation and learning in such contexts. Between May 2022 and October 2023, we explored the feasibility of using a sensemaking methodological approach to provide near real-time feedback on a large-scale health system innovation. We designed two complexity-informed data collection instruments using the Cognitive Edge SenseMaker® tool, and attempted to: 1) operationalize them across diverse patient populations and providers; and 2) engage with stakeholders in collaborative sensemaking of the insights from the data. Between May 2022 and October 2023, test data yielded 221 patient and 104 provider entries regarding surgical referral experiences. Attempts to scale the data collection instruments within formal healthcare channels to reach a diverse representation of patients and providers were unsuccessful. We pivoted to capture information on the impacts of our enacted data collection strategies. From these efforts, we generated a diagrammatic representation of the sensemaking methodological approach, namely the Illuminate 360°. This approach consists of an iterative cycle: data collection, analysis, monitoring/reflection, decision-making, and action planning. Central to this is the integration of regular sensemaking sessions with relevant parties, which facilitates clarity on the phenomenon of interest and insights for action. While scaling up the methodology through formal channels proved unfeasible within the project’s parameters, our findings offer critical insights into building situational awareness for complex healthcare interventions. We demonstrate that the Illuminate 360° approach, when grounded in implementation science frameworks and theories, can generate the timely, co-created data necessary to inform healthcare improvement and support data-driven decision-making.

Digital-based Islamic Religious Education (IRE) provides opportunities to use learning activity data to understand student engagement and learning outcomes. However, high levels of digital activity do not necessarily indicate deep cognitive engagement or successful learning. This study aims to analyze the use of learning analytics to examine student engagement and learning outcomes in digital-based IRE. It employs a qualitative approach using the library research method. Data were obtained by reviewing relevant literature on learning analytics, student engagement, learning outcomes, and digital-based IRE, and were analyzed descriptively through the identification and synthesis of findings. The results indicate that learning analytics can be used to identify behavioral engagement through access to learning materials, task completion, and participation in assessments, as well as to examine cognitive engagement through students’ understanding of learning materials and the quality of their responses. The use of these data can help educators identify learning difficulties, provide feedback, and determine appropriate instructional follow-up. Nevertheless, the relationship between engagement and learning outcomes must be interpreted cautiously because it is influenced by various factors. Digital activity data are also insufficient to assess all aspects of religious understanding and character development. This study concludes that learning analytics has the potential to support pedagogical decision-making in digital-based IRE, provided that data quality, privacy, and the learning context are taken into account.

Construction safety management still struggles to produce daily safety bulletins (DSBs), structured daily communications that identify site-specific hazards, convey safety protocols, and set preventive measures for workers. Manual DSB creation takes 2-3 hours daily and yields inconsistent quality, with 25% of crews never conducting pretask planning (Olson et al., 2016), diverting safety personnel from field supervision. This study proposes the Lightweight Multi-Agent DSB System (LM-DSB), which integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a locally deployable Large Language Model (LLM) to automate DSB generation on consumer-grade personal computers. LM-DSB coordinates specialized planner, researcher, and writer agents in a hierarchical architecture, enhanced by domain-specific fine-tuning on construction safety documentation and RAG grounding in 37 health, safety, and environment (HSE) documents. A two-phase validation assessed feasibility. Phase 1 comparative evaluation showed the multi-agent RAG system (Llama 3-8B) outperformed all alternative configurations, with strong lexical alignment and coherence (TF-IDF: 0.70, BLEU: 0.39, ROUGE-1: 0.66) and near-complete document generation (length ratio: 1.01 vs. 0.39 for single-agent RAG). Phase 2 expert evaluation (N=40) confirmed practical acceptability (mean scores 3.50-4.20 on a 5-point scale), particularly in regulatory compliance (4.20) and factual accuracy (4.10). The findings show that architectural design enables lightweight models to handle safety-critical documentation on consumer-grade hardware, advancing technology democratization in construction safety management. Limitations include knowledge base scope, language constraints, and lack of field deployment validation; future work should address multimodal integration and workflow adoption.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Quantum technologies (QT) are increasingly being taken up in artistic practices, for example in the form of visual artworks or quantum computer music. However, more comprehensive empirical studies on the temporal development and the different forms of QT-related art are still lacking. Therefore, this study conducted a systematic mapping and classification of QT-related artworks. To this end, a medium-independent corpus was established, and the artworks were classified into four categories: QT-Inspired, QT-Sourced, Simulated QT, and QT-Generated. This classification was LLM-assisted and checked against human-coded reference data as well as through manual review of unclear cases. In total, 281 QT-related artworks from 2010 to August 2025 were identified. The corpus shows a substantial increase in QT-related artworks since 2019, with a considerable share attributed to only a few artists. The different forms of QT relations coexist, while an increasing use of active hardware-based and simulated processes in artistic practices can be documented, particularly since 2021. Although no clear development trajectories between these categories can be identified, the observed development coincides with advances in QT and their improved accessibility. Thus, this study provides an empirical basis for further analyzing the development of QT-related art, the possible emergence of a "quantum art scene," and the reciprocal relationships between art and quantum technologies.

Maritime Information Management (MIM) has emerged as one of the most transformative domains in contemporary maritime operations. As global supply chains become increasingly interconnected, port networks more tightly coupled, and vessel traffic more congested, the maritime sector has moved decisively from a hardware-centric industry to a data-driven ecosystem. At its core, MIM concerns the systematic collection, processing, dissemination, and governance of maritime information to enhance operational efficiency, situational awareness, safety, resilience, and decision-making across ocean-based and coastal systems. It integrates technologies, organisational practices, decision-support tools, and behavioural processes that allow maritime stakeholders – ports, shipping companies, pilots, regulators, and emergency managers – to operate with higher levels of synchronisation and foresight ( Heilig & Voß, 2017 ).

Third-party community-based bots are central to how social platforms such as Discord work. They moderate content, manage roles, play music, and support AI-assisted conversations across millions of servers. Yet when a bot is installed in a server, it can access messages, user profiles, and server metadata concerning members who did not participate in the installation decision, with no standardized way to communicate the associated security and privacy implications. In this paper, we analyze 23,102 third-party Discord bots and 183,142 user reviews spanning 49 detected languages and five years of feedback (2021-2026). We employ LLM-based knowledge distillation and fine-tune a DeBERTa-based classifier to identify candidate security and privacy (S&P)-relevant reviews. After manually validating the complete classifier-positive set, we retain 8,832 reviews identified as S&P-relevant, representing an observed pipeline yield of 4.82%, and map them to a 31-theme S&P taxonomy extending prior work. Our results show that S&P-related reviews focus heavily on Data Sharing (30.5%) and Data Collection (16.2%). Confession and anonymity bots have pipeline-identified SPRRs above 50%, more than ten times the ecosystem-wide pipeline yield of 4.82%. Star ratings may obscure the frequency and valence of S&P-related discussion, while conventional metadata features, such as permission count and administrator status, show only weak associations with user-reported S&P concerns. We then build BotLens, a proof-of-concept auditing framework that combines review-derived S&P signals with bot metadata to provide on-demand decision support for the community-based bot ecosystem. BotLens exposes six tools through a Model Context Protocol server, supporting bot-level checkups, server-wide comparison, and integration with AI agents.

As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Every neural-network training run produces not only a model, but also evidence about how models learn. Can these accumulated experiments enable us to predict and compare new training runs before executing them? We study meta-models: models that predict the learning behavior of other models. From this perspective, final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction, and hyperparameter selection are different queries to the same training response function. We take a first, humble empirical step toward this goal: treating real language-model training records as native numeric data, we find that an off-the-shelf tabular in-context learner, TabPFN, can match or outperform a fine-tuned LLM meta-model in multiple evaluated settings. Whereas recent work fine-tunes LLMs on tokenized configurations at a cost of tens to hundreds of GPU-hours, TabPFN requires seconds of fit-and-predict time without task-specific weight updates. We argue that meta-modeling is better treated as its own numeric modality rather than as a text task for LLMs. Going one step further, augmenting TabPFN with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) further improves accuracy on selected prediction tasks. Finally, we pre-registered a forecast of the Marin Hero Run, a 535B-parameter public training run, whose ground truth is revealed point by point as training progresses, putting meta-model predictions to the test against training outcomes not yet observed at the time of forecasting.

This study evaluated energy expenditure while walking with a powered ankle exoskeleton in middle-aged adults. Participants wore a bilateral ankle exoskeleton. Metabolic cost was measured via indirect calorimetry. Participants walked on a treadmill without the exoskeleton and with the exoskeleton unpowered, powered, and unpowered again. Net metabolic cost of transport (MCOT) was calculated. Behaviors exhibited include a decrease in MCOT, an increase in MCOT, and initial changes that diminished with time. This variability may be explained by differences in adaptation times, which may be more pronounced among middle-aged adults due to age-related changes in gait and declines in neuromuscular and sensory function. These results underscore the importance of age-related considerations in training protocols, recognizing that middle-aged adults may require longer, more structured training than young adults. Insufficient adaptation may prevent users from experiencing metabolic improvements that could contribute to reduced injury risk and lower rates of musculoskeletal disorders.

The growing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into human cognitive activities, including problem-solving, decision-making, learning and information processing, has raised important questions about cognitive work allocation, metacognitive control and independent performance. Although GenAI can enhance efficiency by reducing cognitive demands, excessive reliance may weaken users’ engagement in reasoning, verification and independent task execution. This review examines the relationship between GenAI use and human cognition, with particular emphasis on cognitive offloading, appropriate reliance, over-reliance, automation bias and independent performance. Drawing on existing research, it explores how the effects of cognitive offloading depend on task characteristics and the distribution of cognitive responsibility between users and AI systems. The review further considers interventions such as think-first strategies, cognitive forcing functions, reflection, verification prompts and adaptive scaffolding that aim to preserve human cognitive engagement while benefiting from AI assistance. In addition, it examines behavioural telemetry including prompt intent, interaction timing, response editing and verification activities as a potential means of identifying patterns of engagement and reliance during multi-turn human AI interactions. These observable behaviours are treated as indirect indicators rather than definitive measures of internal cognitive processes. The review highlights the importance of evaluating not only task performance with AI assistance but also users’ ability to perform independently when such assistance is unavailable. It identifies a need for integrated frameworks that connect cognitive work allocation, metacognition, observable interaction patterns, reliance calibration and independent performance over time. Such frameworks may support the development of human-centred GenAI systems that improve task effectiveness while maintaining users’ critical thinking, self-regulation and cognitive autonomy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) tutors remove exactly the effort that learning requires: students adopt the instant answer, offload the reasoning to the model, and retain less. Friction-based tutors reverse the offloading, yet learners disengage from unbounded friction. This paper tests whether game-structural mechanics—checkpoints, low-stakes failure with retry, and a rescue that guarantees completion—hold the learner inside a tutor's deliberate friction. In a multi-agent simulation of 180 students (three independent draws of 60) across six levels of seeded misconception burden, each student works the same ten-part physics problem under three tutor conditions: instant answer, strict Socratic, and a ten-checkpoint quest in which every part is unlocked only by the student's own attempt. The quest condition removes the measured offloading: students produce 0.999 of the solution steps against 0.302 under the instant answer, self-reported offloading is 1.48 versus 5.58 on a 6-point scale, and every student names the instant-answer condition as the one in which they offloaded most. Structuring the friction also removes its cost: quest sessions complete in 100 percent of cases, against a 14.4 percent abandonment rate in the strict condition, where sessions that run long end when the student's reported motivation reaches the floor. Both friction conditions raise the unaided posttest far above the shared pretest (0.928 and 0.885 versus 0.455); the instant-answer condition reaches only 0.563. Friction that is structured as bounded progression holds the learner inside productive struggle without the attrition that plain withholding carries.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Social value creation is a stated priority in commercial property and ESG agendas, yet little is known about why owners and occupiers pursue social initiatives or what sustains them. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT) and its sub-theory of organismic integration, this study examines the motivations underpinning social value in Auckland's prime office market, New Zealand. Eleven semi-structured interviews with eighteen owners, occupiers and agents across ten organisations were analysed thematically alongside corporate sustainability reporting. Motivations cluster around four drivers: market obligations, environmental imperatives, employee priorities and socio-cultural responsibilities. These range from external and introjected regulation through identified and integrated forms to, rarely, intrinsic motivation. Owners span the full range, whereas occupiers stabilise at identified regulation centred on employee well-being and organisational culture. This difference is positional rather than dispositional, since participants holding both roles express different motivations depending on the role from which they speak. Motivation also varies spatially: provision closest to the leasing transaction is the most externally regulated and provision furthest from it the most integrated. The study extends motivational theory to the commercial built environment, proposes a dual-stakeholder framework, and shows why assessments based on whether provision exists cannot distinguish durable from compliance-driven social value.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The management of occupational health and safety measurement equipment in educational institutions often faces challenges related to borrowing and returning records, calibration tracking, and access to equipment information, resulting in inefficient management. This research and development study aimed to develop an integrated web-based occupational health and safety measurement equipment management system combining QR Code-based equipment identification, equipment lifecycle management, and LINE Messaging API communication, and to evaluate system quality, user satisfaction, and factors associated user acceptance. The participants consisted of three groups: three personnel involved in equipment management, three information technology experts, and thirty system users.
