Then, we organize the literature around six core dimensions: inference-time planning and execution, training and trajectory construction, safety and control, efficiency under resource constraints, capability completeness in open environments, and benchmark design and evaluation. We further summarize representative applications in software engineering, enterprise workflows, graphical user interfaces, and mobile systems. Finally, we discuss major challenges and outline future directions for building reliable, scalable, and verifiable multi-tool agents.

What keeps a society stable when the conditions on which it depends are constantly changing? This article develops the argument that the persistence of many social orders relies on recurring interventions. Maintenance, correction and renewal make reliability possible, yet often remain in the background of everyday life. The illusion lies in taking stability for granted and overlooking the conditions that sustain it. This relationship becomes particularly apparent under conditions of digitalisation. Algorithms influence which information becomes visible, while generative AI helps shape expressions and interpretations. Digital procedures can facilitate access while also creating new barriers. In this way, possibilities for action change even as the familiar surface of an order remains intact. This theoretical and conceptual article brings together sociological and philosophical approaches with selected empirical studies and thought examples. At its centre is the question of which order interventions sustain, whom it serves and who bears their consequences. The article develops criteria for responsible stabilisation: reliability must be accompanied by decisions that can be justified, effective opportunities to challenge them and a willingness to revise them. Choosing not to intervene can also be part of such an approach. Keywords: stability; social order; intervention; form; responsibility; sociotechnical systems; sociology; philosophy

Many researchers have sought to integrate the interpretive depth of qualitative analysis with the analytical rigor of quantitative methods. We present The Interactive Thematic Analysis Network (TITAN), a novel software platform and methodological framework that extends completed thematic analyses through interactive network visualization and quantitative structural analysis. TITAN automatically transforms hierarchical qualitative coding outputs into multilevel node-and-edge networks, computes network metrics for excerpts, codes, themes, and higher-order groupings, and preserves direct traceability to the underlying qualitative evidence. The software was evaluated using a completed qualitative case study conducted for the U.S. Irregular Warfare Center (IWC), demonstrating automated transformation of thematic analysis outputs into an interactive network representation. We describe TITAN’s software architecture, analytical workflow, and analytical capabilities, showing how network science extends conventional thematic analysis by revealing structural relationships not readily identifiable using existing qualitative analysis software.

Reflexivity was built for a researcher whose instruments were of a different kind than her object. That assumption has quietly failed. When a researcher uses a large language model to code griefbots, recommender systems, or synthetic media, instrument and object come from the same technical population, and the properties her codebook detects (retention by default, smoothness, ambiguous reply status) are simultaneously operating inside the coding. I call this her infrastructural position, and it is not a variant of the social position reflexivity has long theorised. Participant objectivation ascends to a meta-level, an ascent available because the researcher is not a case in her own study. Infrastructural position denies the ascent; the move it permits is lateral. Against the regress objection, catalogued in the sociology of scientific knowledge three decades ago and unresolved there, I distinguish two ambitions. The completeness model seeks self-transparency and is destroyed by the regress. The calibration model is not, because it claims no epistemic privilege at all: it replaces transparency with auditability, and replaces a terminus with a published claim-to-level dependency map. This concedes Lynch’s case against reflexivity as a source of privileged knowledge and reconstructs a method on the far side of it. I demonstrate the model with tool-as-case: turning the algorithm audit on the auditor’s own instrument, under criteria published in object-facing form first. The sharpest consequence is not that model-assisted omission is uncheckable, true of human coding too, but that it is correlated across every study using the same model.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study was conducted to examine the effect of Game-Based Learning (GBL) on students’ intrinsic motivation, behavioral engagement, and emotional engagement, as well as the mediating role of intrinsic motivation in these relationships. The study was prompted by the phenomenon of learning loss following the COVID-19 pandemic, which has led to a decline in motivation and engagement among students at SMKN 2 Kota Kediri. A quantitative approach using SEM-PLS analysis was employed, with a questionnaire serving as the data collection instrument. The theoretical framework used is Self-Determination Theory (SDT) by Ryan & Deci. The study found that GBL has a significant positive effect on intrinsic motivation (f² = 1.328), behavioral engagement (f² = 0.382), and emotional engagement (f² = 0.109). Intrinsic motivation was found to have a significant effect on emotional engagement, but not on behavioral engagement. Mediation analysis indicated that intrinsic motivation partially mediates the effect of GBL on emotional engagement, whereas on the behavioral engagement pathway, intrinsic motivation was not found to act as a mediator. These findings imply that GBL is a learning method considered effective in enhancing learners’ motivation and engagement.

Driver behavior on public roadways requires closer attention to how self-monitoring, attentional control, and individual differences relate to unsafe driving outcomes. This study examined how metacognitive awareness, attentional lapses, mindfulness, temporal focus, and ADHD diagnosis relate to aggressive driving behavior. Participants completed questionnaires assessing metacognitive regulation, cognitive failures, mindfulness, temporal focus, and aggressive driving behavior. Findings indicated that attentional lapses were the strongest predictor of aggressive driving behavior. ADHD diagnosis was no longer a significant predictor after cognitive and self-regulatory variables were included in the model. These results suggest that aggressive driving behavior was more strongly linked to attentional lapses and monitoring failures than to ADHD diagnosis alone. Overall, the findings from this study suggest that aggressive driving behavior is meaningfully influenced by the combination of cognitive lapses, self-monitoring, and individual driver characteristics. Implications include improved driver assessment tools and attentional regulation training for drivers.

Based on the studies on the Production-Oriented Approach (POA) included in the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and combining bibliometrics with close reading, this paper examines the research characteristics, conceptual evolution, and digital-intelligent turn of this theory. The findings show that POA research has moved from rapid growth into a stage of stable deepening, with core authors and institutions becoming concentrated, and research themes expanding from college English to teaching Chinese to speakers of other languages, less commonly taught languages, textbook development, and intelligent teaching. Centered on the problem of 'separating learning from use,' the theory has refined its teaching principles, hypotheses, and procedures, forming a four-dimensional teaching framework that links learning, use, and assessment in a closed loop, together with a unit-nested teaching procedure. Generative artificial intelligence can empower teaching, yet existing studies are mostly short-cycle, single-course, and small-sample practices. Future research should carry out cross-language and cross-stage long-cycle comparisons, and build a human-machine collaborative assessment system based on classroom production, so as to address problems such as data bias, the weakening of teachers' subjectivity, and technology dependence.

Background: Emergency departments represent a critical point of access to healthcare in Canada, yet escalating pressures from overcrowding are putting patients at increased risk of preventable harm due to increased waiting times. Emergency department waiting rooms are evolving from passive holding spaces to extensions of the clinical care environment however, these spaces are not optimized to facilitate patient safety (Zamani, 2019), putting vulnerable individuals waiting for care at risk of deterioration and adverse outcomes. Waiting room safety netting emerges as a nascent, fragmented idea in the literature yet lacks the specificity and contextual grounding to be operationalized to quality improvement initiatives and patient safety planning. This study aimed to explicate the concept of an ED Waiting Room Safety Net utilizing Rodger’s evolutionary concept analysis to identify the antecedents, attributes and consequences of this construct to inform a systems-oriented, contextually adaptable model for patient safety in emergency care. Methods: Rodger’s evolutionary concept analysis was chosen as the method focuses on concepts emerging through praxis rather than discrete conceptualization acknowledging that meaning arises through practice. Concept analysis occurs through six phases: identifying the concept and related terms, selecting the context and sample for data collection, gathering relevant data, analyzing for attributes, antecedents, and consequences, identifying an exemplar, and determining implications for future development. Results: 52 studies were identified through PubMed using combinations of surrogate terms, 18 scholarly works between 2017 and 2025, were selected and synthesized to derive the antecedents, attributes and consequences of a waiting room safety net. The Waiting Room Safety Net can be defined as: A proactive, responsive, and structured patient safety construct that involves optimizing human factors, technology, organizational processes, and the physical environment such that they interact to facilitate protective oversight of individuals in the emergency department waiting room and enable the avoidance of preventable harm while making the waiting experience more amenable to patients. The synthesis of 18 studies revealed eight thematic attributes which were consolidated into a conceptual model. Implications and lessons learned: A waiting room safety net emphasizes the balanced integration of human oversight, technological innovation and adaptive, aligned organizational processes. Fundamental processes include structured surveillance, clear communication, accountability and escalation pathways. This model offers a systems-thinking informed scaffold for waiting room patient safety and quality improvement initiatives.

People living with dementia are one of the populations most at risk of restrictive intervention during an acute hospital admission. These restrictive interventions are typically justified by staff concerns about patient safety and as a means of mitigating against falls, itself a key metric of quality care in acute settings. Drawing on Jasanoff and Kim’s concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, this paper explores how healthcare professionals imagine risk and safety, and how these imaginaries contour the use of restrictive practice. Data collection comprised 225 days of ethnographic observation and 1168 in situ interviews with patients, families, and ward staff at (n = 6) NHS Trusts working in (n = 3) dyads for acute and mental health care across England. Data were analysed thematically using NVivo. Findings were grouped into three major themes: institutional cultures, institutional anxiety, and atrocity stories. The study reveals tensions between ways in which people living with dementia respond to admissions and the institutional imaginaries of a safe, risk-free ward, alongside expectations of “good patienthood.” It argues that these imaginaries produce dementia as a risk classification, where bed or bedside-bound patients who do not demand staff attention inform the routine use of restrictive practices. These interventions, however, often result in distress and feelings of imprisonment among people living with dementia, which in turn prompts further tightening of restraints on this vulnerable population.

The internal structure of hadrons is governed by nonperturbative Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and is being probed with increasing precision by modern high-energy experiments. This dissertation presents first-principles calculations of partonic observables using lattice QCD together with effective field theory methods, with controlled systematic uncertainties, advancing from collinear structure to transverse-momentum-dependent distributions (TMDs) that encode the three-dimensional partonic structure of hadrons. Within the large momentum effective theory (LaMET) framework, this work presents state-of-the-art calculations of pion distribution amplitudes and systematic studies of nucleon parton distributions, with control of renormalization, excited-state contamination, Fourier-transform systematics, and power corrections. A Coulomb-gauge formulation of quasi-distributions is implemented to simplify ultraviolet structure by avoiding Wilson-line related linear divergences. Systematic effects associated with Gribov copies are quantified and found to be negligible at current statistical precision, supporting the effectiveness of this approach. Building on these developments, this dissertation reports first-principles lattice determinations of key TMD quantities, including nucleon TMD parton distributions, the Collins-Soper kernel, the intrinsic soft function, and pion TMD observables. These results provide nonperturbative inputs directly relevant to global QCD analyses and to the precision hadron-structure program at current and future facilities, including the Electron-Ion Collider. In parallel, this dissertation explores machine-learning acceleration of lattice gauge simulations through neural field transformations embedded in Hybrid Monte Carlo. In two-dimensional U(1) tests, the method significantly reduces autocorrelation and improves performance toward finer lattice spacing. Such gains support precision-controlled partonic calculations by enabling finer lattices and larger hadron boosts, thereby reducing LaMET power corrections and improving control of discretization effects. The dissertation also outlines emerging directions using AI agents and foundation models to advance lattice data-analysis workflows under physics-based constraints.
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

documents.abstract: Ant International accumulates large volumes of transaction history across users and payment businesses. Confirmed fraud and chargeback outcomes, by contrast, are scarce, delayed, and specific to each business. A single encoder pretrained on unlabeled histories could serve all businesses, but only if pretraining captures the behavior that separates risk. Coarse activity differences can make contrastive pretraining on transaction logs too easy: transaction volume, amount, and timing can distinguish a history's continuation from arbitrary candidates without modeling how payment resources are used. We present TRIDENT-Seq, a transaction foundation model trained with Prefix-Future Contrast (PFC). PFC matches each prefix to a summary of its subsequent behavior among candidates with similar activity profiles; activity prediction and dispersion regularization act on the encoder output. Across three production payment businesses, the pretrained encoder improves average precision (AP) and recall at a 0.5% intervention budget over architecture-matched scratch training in all six business-budget settings. With a fixed validation set, it exceeds full-label scratch training in mean AP and recall using 10% of the training labels on Wallet and 25% on Shopping and SME. Pretraining only on another business's histories still helps. Replacing profile-matched candidates with random ones cuts recall from 24.62% to 5.64%. In Ant International's deployment evaluation, recorded amount-based chargeback and overall loss rates are 37.7% and 37.9% lower than those of the previous XGBoost-based system under the same intervention budget.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has developed rapidly in recent years. Beyond its specialized domains, it has also been applied to an increasing range of other fields. Prior research suggests that traditional financial decisions are typically reached through investors' own judgment, and that such judgment is readily subject to interference from human factors and other considerations, which compromises the accuracy of the resulting decisions. In response, many developers have introduced AI into the financial industry and integrated it with investment services, giving rise to a novel form of advisory known as robo-advising, or intelligent investment advisory. Robo-advising not only breaks with the conventional human-based advisory model through AI technologies, but also helps investors make more effective decisions, thereby reducing potential losses. Existing studies have proposed that the perceived usefulness of robo-advisory technology affects users' attitude and usage intention, and that information transparency likewise affects users' attitude and usage intention, with attitude positively related to usage intention. However, relatively few studies have examined trust as a mediating mechanism through which these factors shape investors' intention to use robo-advisory. Accordingly, this study employs correlation analysis, regression analysis, and structural equation modeling to analyze the data collected from a questionnaire survey and to test the proposed hypotheses. The findings indicate that the perceived usefulness and information transparency of robo-advising are capable of establishing investor trust, and that such trust can alter investors' attitude toward robo-advising, thereby enhancing their usage intention. In addition, this study aims to offer more effective recommendations for robo-advisory technology and to support the continued development of robo-advisory investment services.

Artificial intelligence (AI) now selects, personalises, writes and voices marketing communications, placing an algorithmic agent at the interface between firms and consumers. Yet the evidence on how consumers respond is fragmented across three largely separate literatures — studies of AI disclosure, of personalisation and privacy, and of algorithm appreciation and aversion — which imply conflicting managerial defaults. This paper integrates these literatures through a single interpretive mechanism drawn from the Persuasion Knowledge Model: persuasion-knowledge activation. We argue that interface design choices — whether AI involvement is disclosed, whether data collection is overt or covert, how humanlike the agent appears, and how the task is framed — do not act on trust directly. They act by changing what consumers infer about the persuader's goals and competence, an inference process in which privacy calculus, uniqueness neglect and identity threat also operate. The resulting Trust at the Interface framework links interface signals to consumer appraisals, to trust attributions directed separately at the AI system and at the firm, and to behaviour, and adds a failure-and-repair loop explaining asymmetric blame and recovery after AI errors. Seven formal propositions specify the framework's testable claims, with implications for interface design, consumer protection and future research.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: As service robots are increasingly deployed in eldercare settings, trust calibration following robot errors has become a core issue affecting the effectiveness of human-robot collaboration. Focusing on older adult users, this study systematically investigates the joint influence mechanism of error situations and explanation strategies on trust calibration through a 2 (error severity: high vs. low) × 2 (transparency: high vs. low) mixed-design experiment, and further tests a cognitive–emotional dual-path model of trust calibration. Using video-based scenario simulation combined with scale-based measurement, the study was conducted with 80 older adults. Results show that high-severity errors significantly undermine both cognitive trust and emotional trust, with a more pronounced detrimental effect on cognitive trust. Transparency interventions primarily facilitate trust repair through the emotional trust pathway, with no significant direct effect on cognitive trust. The study further reveals that transparency is more effective in repairing trust under low-severity error conditions, and that individuals' technology anxiety significantly attenuates the repair efficacy of transparency on the cognitive pathway. These findings not only provide preliminary empirical evidence for a dual-path dissociation pattern in older adults' trust repair—characterized by emotional priority and cognitive lag—but also offer an important empirical basis and design directions for developing age-appropriate service robots with context-awareness, emotional interaction, and personalized adaptation capabilities.

Large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated by final-output correctness or safety, yet an endpoint label does not reveal how a failure develops throughout the reasoning process. We therefore ask whether ordinary reasoning failures and adversarially induced failures can be characterized using the same internal coordinates. Towards this end, we in this paper study a white-box diagnostic framework CauTrace to disclose the root-cause of why LLM fails from three fundamental inspections: Functional States, Propagation of Representation, Temporal-State Coordination and Reasoning Trajectory. First, seven functional states are creatively defined to represent the support and constraint processing in LLMs. Second, the propagation of representation change measures how the changes among the seven states persist across subsequent Transformer blocks. Third, temporal-state coordination and trajectory topology characterize when the commitment and verification occur relative to the support, and how the dominant state sequence evolves over the full inference process. Finally, we evaluate CauTrace on both clean reasoning failures and paired adversarial perturbations. Across Qwen and LLaMA-family models, the failed traces show weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment, while the exact representation-level signatures and timing shifts vary by architecture. Held-out repair and steering tests demonstrate consistent operational signals that were in line with our claims for certain models and specific settings, with aligned steering producing the predicted directional changes in process measures. Overall, CauTrace provides a unified diagnostic framework for analyzing failure dynamics through changes in support, commitment, and verification, which would shed light on the in-depth research on LLM security.

The hybrid work trend in the post-COVID period has transformed how people communicate while at work. However, there is a lack of quantitative understanding of how home and office environments shape communicative behavior and affective well-being. To study this, as a part of a larger study of the role of work environment on stress, we designed an egocentric wearable audio sensing system that captured interpersonal communication across both working locations. The system extracts real-time acoustic features on a wearable audio sensor and performs offline foreground speaker diarization to derive speaking load and activeness features. To improve diarization performance under low-dimensional feature constraints, we apply a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework that transfers knowledge from large-scale speech foundation models into a compact ResNet-based model, achieving consistent improvements in diarization performance over the baseline across three public egocentric speech datasets. In a four-month longitudinal deployment with 16 participants, our system revealed location-dependent differences in work communication patterns. Moreover, the mixed linear model analyses showed that office-based speaking load was significantly associated with higher self-reported stress and lower self-reported productivity, while speaking activeness during home-based work amplified both productivity and affective load in this cohort.

Generative AI (GenAI) has spread unevenly across Europe, and it is unclear whether higher use brings higher trust. This paper compares Denmark and Romania, the EU's highest and lowest GenAI users, and asks whether the difference in public and institutional trust between them corresponds to the difference in trust in AI. Drawing on trust, technology-acceptance and digital-divide theory, it is a descriptive, contrasting-case analysis of harmonised data: GenAI usage comes from Eurostat, trust in AI more generally from the KPMG/Melbourne global study and public and institutional trust from the Standard Eurobarometer. In 2025, 48.4% of Danes aged 16-74 had used GenAI in the past three months, against 17.8% of Romanians. Use falls with age and rises with education in both countries, and the relative gaps are far larger in Romania; the patterns remain visible within the published age-by-education categories. Trust in AI does not follow usage: Romanians trust AI as much as Danes or slightly more, although Denmark leads by 28 to 45 percentage points on trust in government, parliament and the legal system. The Denmark-Romania comparison thus does not support a simple country-level correspondence between general institutional trust and trust in AI; in KPMG's pooled model, trust in AI is tied most closely to confidence in AI governance. The observed usage difference is more consistent with disparities in general digital skills and opportunities for work- and education-related use than with differences in trust. However, the available data cannot identify the independent effects of these factors. The results rest on two cases and non-identical constructs, and call for comparable microdata and disclosure experiments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose The population of older adults is growing rapidly and “ageing-in-place” has become the dominant living arrangement in India. Yet residential interiors in urban environments for older adults continue to be designed on Western anthropometric standards that overlook the physical and cultural needs of older Indians. This study aims to be a preliminary examination of the spatial ergonomics of the “Critical Triad” of kitchen, bedroom and toilet in urban homes in Tamil Nadu, India. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-method study was conducted with 30 participants (24 elderly and 6 middle-aged occupants) across Coimbatore, Salem and Vellore cities of Tamil Nadu, India. Data were collected through on-site spatial measurement, behavioural mapping, semi-structured interviews and expert photography and analysed using prevalence ranking and chi-square tests of association. Findings The study found extensive body-space mismatch rooted in Western-derived design dimensions. Ninety percent of elderly women reported physical strain while working in modular kitchens, 87% of participants lived with fear of falling in toilets and all participants reported discomfort from glossy bedroom flooring and inadequate circulation space. Chi-square analysis confirmed that several kitchen hazards (grinder use, prolonged standing, slippery flooring) are significantly gendered, while bedroom and toilet hazards affect both genders comparably. The erosion of traditional South Indian features such as verandas, detached toilets and semi-open kitchens was linked to heightened safety anxiety and physical dependency. Originality/value The study derives age-adjusted anthropometric benchmarks from National Institute of Design data and translates them into measurable architectural parameters and room layouts for the Critical Triad, offering designers an evidence-based, culturally grounded framework for age-responsive housing in South India.
topics: Aging, Elder Care, and Social Issues
Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) aims to evaluate the perceptual visual quality of images. Recently, the rapid development of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has significantly advanced the IQA field. By integrating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and reinforcement learning (RL), these models can generate more accurate and interpretable results while relying on less training data. However, existing MLLM-based methods are predominantly constrained to holistic, image-level evaluations and lack the capability to produce fine-grained, localized assessments, which substantially limits their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose VGIQA, a novel IQA model endowed with both local and global quality assessment capabilities. VGIQA is trained via a two-stage paradigm comprising a cold-start phase followed by reinforcement learning. Driven by carefully designed local quality assessment reward functions, our model exhibits exceptional image quality understanding on VGSR-2K, a new dataset we propose specifically for local quality evaluation, significantly outperforming existing open-source MLLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct. Furthermore, the local quality evaluation task can effectively enhance the model's performance on the degradation perception task.

ABSTRACT We present vibe‐qc , a general‐purpose open‐source electronic‐structure code for molecules and solids, developed almost entirely with agentic AI under expert human direction. The code is released under the Mozilla Public License 2.0 (MPLv2). The implementation comprises a C++17 numerical core and Python calculation drivers. Molecular methods include Hartree–Fock, Kohn–Sham DFT, Møller–Plesset theory and double hybrids, coupled cluster, active‐space methods, and excited states. Dispersion corrections, continuum solvation, and effective core potentials are also available. Periodic calculations use Gaussian‐basis HF and DFT with Brillouin‐zone sampling. Molecular and periodic method coverage differs; the feature matrices specify analytic and numerical derivatives and distinguish validated and experimental implementations. The validation set is a key contribution of this work. It combines independent program comparisons, published benchmarks, and internal consistency tests. Molecular mean‐field energies agree at the nanohartree scale, and conventional CCSD(T) energies agree within for the tested systems. Local‐correlation and periodic limitations are reported with the comparisons. Numerical results, calculation metadata, and analysis scripts are supplied as machine‐readable . The independently maintained vibe‐view viewer, vibe‐queue scheduler, and qvf toolkit support visualization and job management; trexio provides wavefunction interchange.
topics: Advanced Physical and Chemical Molecular Interactions

documents.abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Virtual fencing (VF) and herding (VH) technologies are revolutionising the management of grazing cattle. These technologies use GPS-enabled collars to manage and contain cattle primarily with audio or vibration cues to guide behaviour, followed by electric shocks if the primary cues are ignored. This reduces the need for electric or physical fencing and decreases the labour required to move animals. This chapter reviews the development, application, and welfare implications of VF and VH technologies. Research and commercial experience demonstrate the effectiveness of the technology, with benefits including improved pasture utilisation, animal productivity, environmental stewardship, labour efficiency, and workforce satisfaction. New technologies must also demonstrate that they at least preserve, if not improve, animal welfare. VF technologies must include proper training regimes based on learning theory, safeguards to prevent the receipt of unpredictable or uncontrollable shocks, and be of an appropriate ergonomic design.

Radiology has evolved with technological innovation, and virtual reality (VR) is an emerging tool in diagnostic imaging workflows. This pictorial essay explores VR-based workstations and virtual monitors in radiology. It describes how immersive environments may complement conventional reading rooms. VR head-mounted displays (HMDs) enable customizable three-dimensional workspaces where radiologists can view multiple virtual monitors, modify spatial layouts, and collaborate remotely in real time. Current applications, including web-based picture archiving and communication system (PACS) platforms and integrated remote desktop functionality, demonstrate the utility of image visualization and interpretation in immersive environments.Potential advantages include workspace flexibility, portability, reduced physical space requirements, and remote collaboration.However, important limitations include display resolution, luminance performance, field of view, image legibility, visual fatigue, and limited validation for diagnostic interpretation.Although preliminary evidence suggests comparable diagnostic performance between VR and conventional monitors for selected imaging tasks, available studies are limited.As VR technology evolves, immersive workstations may become complementary tools within radiology workflows and teleradiology environments.Further research is needed to assess diagnostic accuracy, ergonomic effects, workflow efficiency, user comfort, and cost-effectiveness before broader clinical implementation, and to establish appropriate technical standards for safe, reliable use in routine clinical practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large language models into compact students that preserve aggregate metrics, yet the mechanistic consequences of depth-reduction distillation remain largely uncharacterized. This work applies linear CKA, logit lens analysis, attention pattern decomposition, sparse autoencoder feature statistics, and activation patching to compare GPT-2 and its six-layer student DistilGPT-2 across two canonical circuits: the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) circuit and the Greater-Than (GT) circuit. The results reveal a compression-collapse dichotomy: the IOI circuit suffers complete mechanistic collapse (DistilGPT-2: 35.2% accuracy vs. 94.8%, zero name-mover preservation), while the GT circuit survives with 87.7% task performance recovery through active remapping of the teacher's layer-9 comparison head into student layer~4 (mean Pearson r = 0.945). These findings demonstrate that circuit compressibility governs mechanistic survival under distillation, and that aggregate metrics are insufficient diagnostics for circuit integrity.

Attack logs and red-team reports show targets the attacks used against them, to help them repair their defenses. Prompt injections against large language models (LLMs) are plain text, so such records also hand targets a working copy. Drawing on social learning theory and work on the victim-offender overlap, we study what targets do with that copy in Tensor Trust, an online game whose players defended LLM-guarded accounts, attacked one another's, and could read every attack they received. Using all 563,349 attack records, we compare each received attack with matched attacks that circulated among similar players at the same moment but never reached the target. Reuse mainly followed success: within a week, targets attacked other players with 10.0% of the attacks that had broken their defense, versus 0.03% of matched attacks (adjusted difference: 8.8-10.0 percentage points). Near-misses, whose replies began with "access granted" but that scored as failures, were reused about as rarely as failures: reuse tracked whether an attack paid off, not how its reply read, consistent with payoff-biased social learning. Breaches were also followed by defense changes, after which same-family attacks became 24.5 percentage points less successful against the target, relative to other defenders. Reuse came mainly from players already attacking, not newcomers. Previously received texts accounted for 23.2% of the successful hijacks we analyze. The attack history thus served both repair and reuse; we derive testable hypotheses for how AI security tools should disclose attacks, such as describing the technique without the full text.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Digital transformation has accelerated the adoption of algorithm-driven work environments, creating significant challenges for workforce management. Therefore, this study examines how algorithmic management affects employees competitive productivity through the mediator of career resilience, while perceived algorithmic fairness acts as the moderator. Using survey data from 475 employees of Malaysian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), this study employs a mixed-method approach, incorporating partial least squares structural equation Modeling for hypothesis testing and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) for additional insights. Our findings confirm that algorithmic management enhances employees competitive productivity through career resilience, with perceived algorithmic fairness strengthening this effect, supported by fsQCA. Practically, SMEs should prioritize transparent algorithmic management and resilience-building initiatives to enhance employee competitive productivity. Theoretically, this study advances sociotechnical systems literature by integrating algorithmic management, resilience, and perceived algorithmic fairness, extending Information Systems research on digital workplaces.
